human_tolerance.notes: The article attributes its spread in Europe to having been introduced to estates and parks, where it breeds at sites with open water and short grass. It is a bold bird that pursues intruders in aerial fights when breeding.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: The source gives no calendar breeding window; both sexes care for the goslings until they can graze themselves, and the species is not described as migrating.

phases.name: dispersal
phases.note: In the northern range the article describes winter as a period of wide dispersal into river valleys, feeding on short grass and cereals.

vocalizations.description: The male has a hoarse, subdued duck-like quack which seldom sounds unless it is aroused, plus a louder breathy call performed in rapid sequence and sounding somewhat like a steam engine. The female has a far noisier raucous quack that frequently sounds in aggression when she is tending her young.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 2498252 from the species/match endpoint and iNaturalist taxon 72486 from the taxa endpoint; the Wikidata QID is the one the English article's taxobox links to.

conservation.note: The species article's taxobox records IUCN category Least Concern.

range.note: The article calls the species 'an African member of the Anatidae family' and gives no list of African countries for the native range, so only ZA is recorded rather than inventing a country set. The seven introduced countries are all named individually in the article: it is established in Britain, the United States, Mauritius, Israel and the United Arab Emirates, and was introduced to Australia and New Zealand without becoming established.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Walk and Fly follow from a goose that 'feed on short grass and cereals' and that chases intruders into aerial dogfights; Swim follows from the article's description of goslings feeding on small aquatic invertebrates and freshwater plankton.

traits.flight.note: 'Both sexes are aggressively territorial towards their own species when breeding, and frequently pursue intruders into the air, attacking them in aerial dogfights.'

traits.nest_type.note: It breeds 'at sites with open water, short grass, and suitable nesting locations (either islands, holes in old trees, or amongst epicormic shoots on old trees)'. The cavity option is recorded as the nest type.

traits.perching.note: A waterfowl that forages on short grass, feeds in river valleys and swims; the article describes no perching, so false is recorded.

traits.mass_kg.note: AVONET Mass 1873 g for Alopochen aegyptiaca, sourced by AVONET to Dunning.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Authored bracket of 1.6-2.2 kg around the AVONET mean, allowing for the sex difference the article notes, the males usually being somewhat larger. No sourced mass range was found; treat as an estimate.

traits.wingspan_m.note: Twice the AVONET Wing.Length of 356 mm, rounded to 0.712 m. AVONET does not give a wingspan directly.

traits.shoulder_height_m.note: Authored. The schema describes this field for four-legged animals, and no source gives a standing height for this species; 0.35 m is a judgement from a 0.68 m long goose with legs that reach the ground, and it can be left out of the simulation for a waterfowl.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Honest gap. Neither the species article, Wikidata nor GBIF gives a wild longevity figure for this species, and no openly licensed source with one was found. 12 years is an authored placeholder for a large waterfowl; it is not a sourced value.

traits.diet.note: 'they feed on short grass and cereals' for the adults, and goslings 'feed largely on small, aquatic invertebrates, especially freshwater plankton' until strong enough to graze. The 0.6/0.25/0.15 split is authored from those two statements; the source gives no proportions.

traits.senses.note: Authored: diurnal waterfowl with coloured vision and modest olfaction.

traits.social.note: 'Egyptian geese usually mate for life. Both the male and female care for the offspring.' The upper bound of 8 is authored; the source gives no group size.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Recorded as diurnal: forages by day on grass and in river valleys, with no nocturnal behaviour described.

traits.defense.note: Mob. 'Both sexes are aggressively territorial towards their own species when breeding, and frequently pursue intruders into the air, attacking them in aerial dogfights'; the female's raucous quack is used in aggression when tending young.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement from a bird that holds established breeding populations on estates and parks alongside people and attacks rather than withdrawing.

habitat.use.note: AVONET gives Habitat Wetland and Primary.Lifestyle Generalist, and the article says the bird is 'found in open or semiopen habitats, typically near fresh water, ranging from lowlands to 4000 m above sea level'. The 0.5 ground / 0.3 aquatic / 0.2 aerial split is authored from grass feeding, swimming and aerial chasing.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Derived from the habitat sentence: a bird of open water and short grass, resting on the ground or water rather than in cover.

habitat.resources.note: The graze, invertebrate and seed tags map onto the diet statements in the article; water and pond follow 'typically near fresh water' and the nesting sites 'with open water'; cavity follows the holes in old trees. Weights are authored.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Exploiter, dist_building_min_m and uses_gardens are sourced from the passage on introduction to estates and parks and on range expansion in Europe; impervious_max, light_max and road_mortality are authored.

seasonal.strategy.note: The article describes no migration for the native range and records winter dispersal rather than movement away, so ActiveYearRound is recorded by inference from the absence of any stated migration.

seasonal.phases.note: The article gives no calendar breeding window, so the breeding phase spans the year. The winter dispersal window is stated for the northern range as December to February and is recorded as such; it is not the Western Cape pattern.

seasonal.life_stages.note: The egg stage and its cavity requirement follow the nesting locations in the article. The 60-day juvenile duration and 0.65 scale are authored; the source says only that the goslings feed on aquatic invertebrates 'until they are a few weeks old and strong enough to graze'.

vocalizations.song.note: Both sexes' voices are described in one paragraph: the male's hoarse subdued quack, his louder breathy rapid-sequence call like a steam engine, and the female's noisier raucous quack.

look.note: The article gives a partial description: the sexes are identical in plumage but the males are usually somewhat larger, tone varies from grey to browner birds, and 'a large part of the wings of mature birds is white, but the white is hidden by the wing coverts when at rest' and displayed when aroused, so the white is placed on the outer wing panels. The grey-brown body tone, dark eye patch and proportions are authored.

behavior.note: Mostly authored for the shared ground-forager program, which the article's behaviour supports: a bird that walks on short grass to graze, swims and flies, and flushes into flight when threatened. flee_gait fly, food_tag graze and the daylight rest window are authored from that. The shared program is not mammal-specific in its logic, and a reptile record in this repository already uses it.
